source.title: LOPS: Learning Order Inspired Pseudo-Label Selection for Weakly Supervised Text Classification
source.authors: Dheeraj Mekala; Chengyu Dong; Jing-Bo Shang

record.tranche_reason: Tests learning order for clean and incorrectly pseudo-labeled examples in weakly supervised text classification, extending the cited memorization finding to this setting.
record.gate_note: The paper uses naturally occurring heuristic pseudo-label errors, not completely random labels. It reports learning-order results for clean versus wrong labels; other memorization results mentioned in the paper are citations and are not extracted as this study's results.
record.test_reason: The study directly measures when BERT first predicts correct versus incorrect heuristic pseudo-labels, testing V6 in weakly supervised text classification. Its own learning-order observations go beyond evaluating its selection method.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors say their experiments confirm earlier learning of clean samples and later learning of wrong annotations. Their main conclusion is that LOPS provides effective, stable pseudo-label selection and improves many text classifiers and weakly supervised frameworks.
record.recipe_differences: The study measures learning order for heuristic pseudo-labels in weakly supervised text classification; it does not reproduce random-label image training or the original intervention.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported examples and comparison are specific to text datasets and BERT; exact dataset-level learning-order proportions are not stated.

fits_no_version.finding: LOPS improves classification performance in many settings, with reduced performance on a small 20News-Fine subset.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Learning-order-based pseudo-label selection can improve weakly supervised classification, but its benefit depends on having enough selected training examples.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: The learning-order comparison is presented qualitatively without exact proportions in the text. Table 7 provides selected cases rather than a population-level result. The experiments concern heuristic pseudo-label errors, not completely random labels.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant results omitted. Other performance tables evaluate LOPS and competing selection methods on end-to-end classification scores, not the behavior named in V1–V6.

untested.parts: Completely random labeling, near-zero training error, chance test performance, and unchanged architecture and training hyperparameters.
Relative training time for true versus random labels and convergence as corruption increases.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
A random-corruption sweep measuring perfect training fit and steadily worsening test error.
Effects of adding or removing explicit regularization on random-label fitting and true-label generalization.
Completely random labels and learning dynamics outside heuristic pseudo-label text classification; shared-pattern learning is inferred from label correctness rather than separately measured.

missing.what: Dataset-level distributions of first-learned epochs for correct and incorrect initial pseudo-labels on NYT-Fine, 20News-Coarse, 20News-Fine, Books, and AGNews. These provide broader direct evidence than Table 7's selected cases. The supplied text contains axes and legends but does not preserve readable plotted values, so their directions and magnitudes cannot be determined reliably.

record.verdict_notes: Heuristic label errors fall within V6's noisy-label setting but do not test the random-label interventions in V1–V5. No separate NYT-Fine verdict is justified by the selected examples alone.

versions.untested_parts: Does not train on completely random labels or report training and test error for that intervention.
Does not compare time to fit random labels with time to fit true labels, or sweep the fraction of corrupted labels.
Does not train on shuffled pixels, permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Does not sweep random label corruption from none to all while measuring training and test error.
Does not test weight decay, dropout, or data augmentation as interventions on random-label fitting or true-label generalization.

Tests clean versus incorrectly assigned heuristic pseudo-labels in text classification; does not test completely random labels or establish that the learning-order effect holds for other data modalities.

rows.subject: BERT
rows.operation_detail: Compared learning epochs for correctly and incorrectly pseudo-labeled documents during training.
rows.measure: Proportion of correct and wrong instances by earliest epoch learned; text says most clean instances are learned in the first epoch, while wrong instances are learned across all epochs.
rows.value: Most clean instances are learned in the first epoch; wrong instances are learned across all epochs, and the number of wrong instances learned in the first epoch is significantly less.
rows.note: Qualitative comparison; no exact proportions for the learning-order result are stated in the text.
rows.check: The reported population-level trend supports earlier learning of clean labels; qualitative reporting alone does not make the effect partial. Correct the locator to Introduction, Figure 1(b). The statement about significantly fewer wrong instances compares learning-order selection with probability-based selection, not wrong versus clean instances, and does not establish statistical significance for the learning-order difference.

rows.subject: BERT
rows.operation_detail: Compared learning epochs for correctly and incorrectly pseudo-labeled documents during training.
rows.measure: Incorrectly pseudo-labeled examples in the displayed cases were learned at later epochs.
rows.value: The displayed incorrectly pseudo-labeled examples were each learned at epoch 2.
rows.note: Case examples only; the table illustrates later learning of wrong pseudo-labels and does not establish a population-level comparison.
rows.check: The four selected wrong-label examples were learned at epoch 2, but Table 7 provides no clean-label comparison or representative sampling. These cases cannot independently establish the learning-order effect. Keep their NYT-Fine condition separate from R1's NYT-Coarse condition.

relationships.condition: BERT on NYT-Coarse with initial heuristic pseudo-labels
relationships.reason: R1 reports that most clean instances are learned in epoch 1 while wrong instances are learned across epochs, supporting the claimed learning-order tendency despite overlap.
relationships.display_finding: Most clean instances were learned in epoch 1, while wrong instances were learned across epochs, with some overlap.
